name: Nootka
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern
earlier_scan.source_named: Wikipedia, Nuu-chah-nulth language (citing Carlson, Esling & Fraser 2001, JIPA) — Nootka gc retired, split into Ditidaht and Nuu-chah-nulth
earlier_scan.note: weight-sensitive stress within initial two-syllable window; default initial when weights tie.

new_statements.quote: Stress is on the first or second vowel of the word. In general, syllable weight determines the placement of stress within this domain; a long vowel receives stress. A syllable with a short vowel and closed by a nonglottalized resonant also counts as heavy. With a sequence of long vowels, or when there are no long vowels present, the default is to stress the first vowel. Particularly in citation forms, it is easier to determine vowel quantity differences than to make judgements about relative prominence. Loudness may coincide with length as a marker of stress, while pitch may vary independently of length and loudness.
new_statements.citation: Carlson, Barry F., John H. Esling & Katie Fraser. 2001. Nuuchahnulth. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 31(2): 275-279. doi:10.1017/S0025100301002092
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: PDF metadata Title 'Nuuchahnulth', Author 'Barry F. Carlson, John H. Esling, Katie Fraser', running head 'Journal of the International Phonetic Association (2001) 31/2', DOI 10.1017/S0025100301002092). Re-extracted PDF page 3 = journal p. 277 with extracted text: the 'Stress' section reads exactly as quoted ('Stress is on the first or second vowel of the word. In general, syllable weight determines the placement of stress within this domain; a long vowel receives stress. A syllable with a short vowel and closed by a nonglottalized resonant also counts as heavy. With a sequence of long vowels, or when there are no long vowels present, the default is to stress the first vowel. Particularly in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is confined to the first two syllables (the initial foot). Stress the first syllable if it is heavy (long vowel, or short vowel + tautosyllabic plain resonant/nasal); if the first is light and the second heavy, stress the second; if both are light or both heavy, stress the first. Equivalent formulations: Stonham 1999 p. 60 rule (10) 'Stress the leftmost heavy syllable within the first foot; if both syllables are light, stress the leftmost one'; Stonham 2004 p. 16 'Stress the first syllable, unless the second syllable is heavier'; Wilson 1986 p. 288; Davidson 2002 p. 25; Kim 2003 p. 144.
new_statements.secondary_stress: JIPA 2001 says nothing. Stonham 1999 p. 61: beyond the first foot 'secondary stress occurs on alternating syllables from the primary stress, following the foot structure', explicitly tentative; Waldie 2003 confirms this for Ahousaht; Wilson 1986 p. 288 found no secondary stresses marked in Sapir's data.
new_statements.exceptions: Waldie 2003 (Ahousaht field data): when the first two syllables have equal weight (#LL, #HH) either syllable may be stressed, i.e. lexically variable stress in addition to the weight rule. Davidson 2002 pp. 25-26: rule accounts for only 73-84% of Sapir's 1924 tokens; coda nasals attract stress in Stonham's/Sapir's Tseshaht data but not consistently in Sapir 1924. Kim 2003 p. 164: in Ahousaht only long vowels are heavy (coda consonants not moraic), contra JIPA 2001 and Stonham. Stonham 1999 p. 60: V?V sequences attract stress and may outrank other heavy syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word = first foot domain), described from citation forms; JIPA notes that vowel quantity is easier to judge than prominence, and that loudness tracks length while pitch varies independently. Dialects: JIPA/Kim/Waldie = Ahousaht; Stonham/Wilson/Davidson = Tseshaht (Sapir's data); Rose 1981 (Kyuquot) silent.
new_statements.identity_note: noot1239 is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping code (ISO 639-3 [noo], split 2011 by change request 2010-033 into Nuu-chah-nulth [nuk] = nuuc1236 and Ditidaht [dtd] = diti1235). The quoted statement describes the Ahousaht dialect of Nuu-chah-nulth (nuuc1236); the Tseshaht dialect (Stonham 1999/2004, Wilson 1986, Davidson 2002 from Sapir's data) has the same rule with coda nasals counted heavy. by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) this should be filed as nuuc1236 (or an alias of it), not as a separate catalog entity; the Ditidaht half has its own, different rule (Werle 2007 CJL pp. 91-92: only long vowels heavy, #LĹ iambic, coda consonants not moraic), already held under diti1235.

new_statements.quote: p. 132: "Wilson maintains that while Northern Wakashan assigns stress over the whole word based on weight, Nootka restricts stress to occurring in the first foot of the word. This suggests that the first foot is some sort of domain for stress assignment". p. 135: "In addition, stress can be assigned to the first foot and appear on the head of the first branching nucleus or it may appear on the first nucleus if neither branches." p. 126: "On the other hand, nasals in Nootka do appear to attract stress, acting as long vowels do in this respect." (28a) nú:taswe?in, ná:csa:ƛwe?in, hawá:taƛwe?in; (28b) čímsmi:t 'Son of Bear', hačímsiqsak?i 'her brothers'.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened and, and independently re-rendered pdf pp. 138, 144, 147 (book pp., image-only scan; the PDF's metadata confirms) and read the page images. The front matter identifies the file as Stonham, Combinatorial Morphology, CILT 120, Benjamins 1994, so the file is the cited work. All three prose quotations are verbatim on the page images: p. 132 §5.2.3.4.3 'Wilson maintains that while Northern Wakashan assigns stress over the whole word based on weight, Nootka restricts stress to occurring in the first foot of the word. This suggests that the first foot is some sort of domain for stress assignment'; p. 135 §5.2.3.6 'In addition, stress can be assigned to the first foot and appear on the head…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statement (Carlson, Esling & Fraser 2001, p. 277: stress on the first or second vowel, weight-determined, long vowel or short vowel + nonglottalized resonant heavy). Stonham adds the first-foot domain framing, the moraic status of resonants under N' (contrasted with Nitinaht/Ditidaht where only vowel length counts), the tie-break that the leftmost heavy syllable wins, the default to the first syllable when both are light, and five marked examples. Stonham's data are from Sapir & Swadesh 1939 / Sapir's field notes (Tsishaath, Alberni), Carlson et al. describe Ahousaht; the rules agree.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls within the first foot, i.e. the first two syllables of the word. Within that window it goes to the first heavy syllable (a 'branching nucleus': a long vowel, or a short vowel plus a tautosyllabic nasal/sonorant, which Stonham treats as moraic under N'); if neither of the first two syllables is heavy, stress falls on the first syllable. When both are heavy the first wins (ná:csa:ƛwe?; čímsmi:t, where a first-syllable VN beats a second-syllable long vowel), and a first-syllable short vowel loses to a second-syllable VN or long vowel (hačímsiqsak?i, hawá:taƛwe?in). The first-foot restriction is attributed to Wilson 1985 (Stress Rules in Wakashan, MA thesis, not accessible). p. 17 n. 15: Kwak'wala scans the whole word left to right, Nootka scans only the first foot; p. 16: in Nitinaht only vowel length counts, in Nootka sonorants also add weight.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions. pp. 122-123 add that stress is independent of the 'variable-length' vowel alternation: 'unstressed vowels are found to occur both long and short, and in any position in the word' and 'variable length vowels do not necessarily correlate with the stressed vowel of a word'. §3.4 (pp. 74-80, Nootka syllable structure) says nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: noot1239 is a retired bookkeeping code (old ISO [noo]) split into Nuu-chah-nulth (nuuc1236) and Ditidaht (diti1235). Stonham 1994's 'Nootka' is Nuu-chah-nulth; his examples come from Sapir & Swadesh 1939 and Sapir's unpublished notes (Tsishaath/Alberni; index also lists Kyuquot Nootka 39n, Tsishaath Nootka 38n). He treats Nitinaht (Ditidaht) separately: same first-foot, weight-based stress but with only vowel length counting as weight (p. 16: 'Nitinaht where only vowel length figures.. Nootka, where N' is the domain and sonorants may also add weight'; p. 17: 'the stress patterns of these two closely related languages differ along these lines').
